docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The block diagram below is the block diagram showing the Gripper and Object Handling subsystem of the Simple Educational Robotic Arm. In this subsystem, the Gripper servo and the sensors’ input signals are controlled by the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano microcontroller. The block diagram includes the power supply lines, signal conditioning, microcontroller I/O ports, and other interfaces of the subsystem with the Arm Motion Control and User Controls & Safety subsystems.

docs.title: Block Diagram Design Explanation
docs.text:
The Gripper and Object Handling subsystem is designed to control the robotic arm's gripper while monitoring the force applied to an object. The block diagram separates the design into power distribution, force sensing, microcontroller control, servo operation, and communication.

Power Distribution: A 9 V external supply provides power through a 1 A fuse to an L7805 linear voltage regulator. The regulator produces a nominal 5 V supply for the external electronics, including the servo gripper and force-sensing circuit. The PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano is powered separately through USB.

Force Sensing: The FSR 402 force sensor produces a resistance change when pressure is applied. The MCP6004 operational amplifier buffers the resulting voltage signal before it reaches the PIC's RA0 analog input. This allows the microcontroller to monitor gripping force.

Gripper Control: The PIC18F57Q43 generates a servo control signal to operate the Kitronik Klaw Mk2 gripper. This allows the subsystem to open and close the gripper to handle objects.

Communication: UART connections are provided for communication with the Arm Motion Control and User Controls & Safety subsystems. These connections are intended to allow coordinated operation between the different sections of the robotic arm.

Debugging and Testing: A debug LED, pushbutton, and test points provide additional interfaces for monitoring and troubleshooting the subsystem.

Design Decisions and Product Requirements: The design uses a servo-operated gripper because it provides straightforward position control without requiring a separate H-bridge motor driver. The FSR 402 adds force-sensing capability, while the MCP6004 provides signal buffering. Separating the power supply, sensor, and control functions makes the design easier to understand and troubleshoot. Together, these features support the robotic arm's requirements for controlled gripping, object handling, and communication between subsystems.

docs.title: Gripper Component Selection
docs.text:
Overview Component Selection Process This page describes the process used to select components for the Gripper & Object Handling subsystem of Team 107's Simple Educational Robotic Arm.

This subsystem relies on a PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano microcontroller to control a servo-mechanized gripper and detect any object through infrared detection and to sense gripper strength through a Force Sensitive Resistor (FSR).

The objective here is to choose low-cost components which would be able to effectively detect and grasp any object as well as to ensure their safe handling.

Total budget for the chosen components is $60. The PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano is already owned and doesn’t need to be purchased.

The following section provides a comparison of alternatives to components in question.

docs.title: Component Selection 1: Gripper Servo Motor
docs.text: The gripper requires a servo motor that can open and close its fingers while remaining compact, affordable, and compatible with the PIC18F57Q43 microcontroller. Three TowerPro servo motors were compared.

docs.title: Table 1: Servo Motor Comparison
docs.text: Solution Advantages Disadvantages Price TowerPro SG90 Lightweight (9 g); inexpensive; PWM controlled; suitable for small grippers Plastic gears can wear or strip; limited torque for heavier objects $4.60 TowerPro MG90S Metal gears improve durability; compact (13.4 g); approximately 1.8 kg·cm stall torque at 4.8 V; PWM controlled More expensive than SG90; limited torque for heavy objects $9.00 estimated TowerPro MG996R Metal gears; approximately 9.4 kg·cm stall torque at 4.8 V; suitable for heavier gripping loads Larger (55 g); requires more current; adds weight to the robotic arm $11.20

docs.title: Selected Component: TowerPro MG90S
docs.text:
Manufacturer: TowerPro

Part Number: MG90S

Operating Voltage: Approximately 4.8–6 V

Control: PWM

Selection Explanation:

The TowerPro MG90S was selected for the Gripper & Object Handling subsystem because it offers a suitable balance of size, cost, durability, and gripping capability. Its metal gears provide better resistance to mechanical wear than the plastic gears of the SG90. Although the MG996R produces significantly more torque, its larger size and weight make it less suitable for a compact educational gripper.

The MG90S can be controlled using a PWM output from the PIC18F57Q43 microcontroller. A separate regulated servo power rail will be used, with a common ground shared with the microcontroller.

The MG90S is the preferred choice pending verification that its torque is sufficient for the intended gripper mechanism and object weight.

docs.title: Component Selection 2: Object Detection Sensor
docs.text: The gripper requires an object detection sensor to determine when an object is positioned near the gripping fingers. Three sensors were compared based on cost, detection capability, circuit complexity, and compatibility with the PIC18F57Q43.

docs.title: Table 2: Object Sensor Comparison
docs.text: Solution Advantages Disadvantages Reference Price Vishay TCRT5000 Compact; low-cost reflective infrared sensing; compatible with a simple transistor interface; suitable for close-range object detection Detection depends on object reflectivity and distance; requires resistors and signal conditioning $3.39 (TCRT5000-based module) Vishay CNY70 Very inexpensive; compact; simple phototransistor output; low component count Very short sensing distance; sensitive to object surface and alignment $0.95 ST VL53L0X with Adafruit breakout Measures distance rather than reflected intensity alone; longer detection range; digital I²C interface More expensive; requires additional firmware; changes the interface used in the existing block diagram $14.95

docs.title: Selected Component: Vishay TCRT5000
docs.text:
Manufacturer: Vishay

Part Number: TCRT5000

Sensor Type: Reflective infrared proximity sensor

Microcontroller Connection: RB5 GPIO input through signal-conditioning circuitry

Selection Explanation:

The Vishay TCRT5000 was selected because it provides a compact and economical method of detecting objects near the gripper fingers. Its reflective infrared sensing method is appropriate for short-range detection, while its phototransistor output can be interfaced with the PIC18F57Q43 using suitable resistors and a pull-up circuit.

The CNY70 is less expensive but has a shorter practical sensing range. The VL53L0X offers more advanced distance measurement but introduces additional cost and firmware complexity.

The TCRT5000 is therefore the preferred choice for this educational robotic gripper. The final sensor position and detection threshold will be tested with the intended objects.

Price Note: The $3.39 reference is for a TCRT5000-based sensor module, not necessarily the bare Vishay TCRT5000. The final bill of materials will use the price of the exact version purchased.

docs.title: Component Selection 3: Grip Force Sensor
docs.text: The gripper requires a force sensor to monitor contact pressure and reduce the risk of damaging objects. Three sensor options were compared based on size, cost, circuit complexity, and compatibility with the PIC18F57Q43.

docs.title: Table 3: Grip Force Sensor Comparison
docs.text: Solution Advantages Disadvantages Price Interlink FSR 402 Thin and lightweight; simple voltage-divider interface; suitable for detecting grip pressure Nonlinear output; not ideal for precise force measurement $2.99 Interlink FSR 400 Compact sensing area; lightweight; compatible with analog measurement Small sensing area; nonlinear output; mounting alignment matters $2.99 SparkFun TAL220 Load Cell Better suited to calibrated force measurements; useful for quantitative force feedback Requires an amplifier or ADC interface; more complicated mechanical mounting $12.95

docs.title: Selected Component: Interlink FSR 402
docs.text:
Manufacturer: Interlink Electronics

Part Number: FSR 402 (30-81794)

Sensor Type: Force-sensitive resistor

Microcontroller Connection: RA0/ANA0 analog input through a voltage divider

Selection Explanation:

The Interlink FSR 402 was selected because it provides a lightweight and relatively inexpensive way to detect gripping pressure. Its thin sensing area can be incorporated into a gripper finger without requiring a complicated mechanical assembly.

The FSR 400 is also compact but has a smaller sensing area. A TAL220 load cell is more appropriate when calibrated force measurement is needed, but it requires additional electronics and mechanical integration.

The FSR 402 is suitable for monitoring relative grip pressure rather than measuring precise force. Its voltage-divider output can be read by the PIC18F57Q43 ADC to help the controller adjust the gripper servo and avoid excessive pressure on objects.

The final resistance values, sensor mounting, and grip thresholds will be established during testing.

docs.title: Component Selection 4: Gripper Mechanism
docs.text: The gripper mechanism must open and close around lightweight objects while remaining compact and affordable. Three commercial mechanisms were compared.

docs.title: Table 4: Gripper Mechanism Comparison

docs.title: Preferred Component: Kitronik Klaw MK2
docs.text:
Manufacturer: Kitronik

Product: Klaw MK2 Robotic Gripper Kit

Reference Price: $11.94

Selection Explanation:

The Kitronik Klaw MK2 is the preferred mechanical gripper because it offers a low-cost servo-operated mechanism suitable for an educational robotic arm. It is more affordable than the other compared options, leaving additional budget for sensors, power regulation, and wiring.

Before finalizing this selection, the team must confirm that the mechanism can accommodate the TowerPro MG90S servo, that the available torque is sufficient, and that the force sensor can be mounted on a gripping surface. If these requirements cannot be met, an alternative gripper mechanism will be selected.

docs.title: Component Selection 5: Power Supply and Voltage Regulation
docs.text:
The Gripper & Object Handling subsystem requires regulated power for the PIC18F57Q43 microcontroller, object detection sensor, force sensor, and servo motor. The design uses a USB power source and must provide a stable supply voltage while maintaining a common ground between components.

Three voltage regulator options were compared based on cost, output current, efficiency, and ease of integration.

docs.title: Table 5: Voltage Regulator Comparison
docs.text: Solution Advantages Disadvantages Reference Price ST L7805CV Linear Regulator Simple circuit; regulated 5 V output; widely available; low electrical noise Requires sufficient input voltage above 5 V; dissipates heat; limited output current Approximately \(1–\)2 Texas Instruments LM2940CT-5.0 Linear Regulator Regulated 5 V output; lower dropout than a traditional 7805; relatively simple circuit Still requires input voltage above 5 V; dissipates heat; capacitor requirements must be followed Approximately \(2–\)4 Pololu D24V22F5 Switching Regulator Regulated 5 V output; high efficiency; suitable for higher current loads More expensive; switching noise; not a linear regulator Approximately \(10–\)15

docs.text:

  • Pololu voltage regulator products

docs.title: Preferred Regulation Approach
docs.text:
External Power Supply: Regulated 5 V DC

Servo Supply: 5 V DC directly from the external supply, provided sufficient current is available

Logic Supply: 3.3 V using a suitable low-dropout linear regulator or the Curiosity Nano's approved onboard power arrangement

Candidate 3.3 V Regulator: Microchip MCP1700-3302 (pending current and board-power verification)

Selection Explanation:

The Gripper & Object Handling subsystem uses a regulated external 5 V DC supply. Because this supply already provides the nominal operating voltage required by the MG90S servo, a separate 5 V regulator is unnecessary. The servo will connect to the 5 V power rail rather than a microcontroller output pin.

The PIC18F57Q43 and associated sensor interfaces will operate at compatible 3.3 V logic levels. A suitable 3.3 V low-dropout linear regulator may be used where an external logic supply is required, subject to verification of the Curiosity Nano board's approved power configuration and total current consumption.

The L7805CV, LM2940, and D24V22F5 were compared as 5 V regulation alternatives, but none is selected to regulate an existing 5 V input to 5 V.

The servo and microcontroller circuits will share a common ground. Power-supply current capacity, decoupling capacitors, and wiring will be verified before construction.

Final Power Approach: External regulated 5 V supply with a compatible 3.3 V logic power arrangement.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This Bill of Materials (BOM) documents the components required for the Gripper and Object Handling subsystem of Team 107's Simple Educational Robotic Arm.

The subsystem uses a Kitronik Klaw Mk2 servo-operated gripper, an FSR 402 force sensor, an MCP6004 operational amplifier, and a PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano microcontroller. The circuit receives a 9 V external power input and uses a voltage regulator to provide a 5 V supply for the gripper electronics, while the microcontroller is powered separately through USB.

The BOM includes component quantities, specifications, manufacturer information, supplier details, estimated prices, and spare components for prototyping and assembly.

The estimated purchasing subtotal is $44.30, excluding shipping and taxes, within the $60 subsystem budget. Separate purchase requests have been prepared for DigiKey and RobotShop USA.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Gripper & Force Sensor Circuit is designed for the Simple Educational Robotic Arm project in EGR 304.

This subsystem controls the robotic arm's gripper servo motor and monitors gripping force using a force-sensitive resistor (FSR 402).

The circuit uses a PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano microcontroller to generate the servo control signal and read the force sensor through an analog input.

An MCP6004 operational amplifier buffers the force sensor signal. A 9 V external power supply and L7805 voltage regulator provide a nominal 5 V supply for the external circuitry.

Additional features include a debug LED, pushbutton, UART interface, and expansion connections.

docs.title: Circuit Functionality
docs.text:
The Gripper and Object Handling subsystem is responsible for opening and closing the robotic arm's gripper while monitoring the force applied to an object.

Force Sensor and Signal Conditioning: The FSR 402 force-sensitive resistor changes resistance when pressure is applied. Together with a 10 kΩ resistor, it produces a voltage that changes with gripping force. The MCP6004 operational amplifier conditions this signal before it reaches the PIC18F57Q43 microcontroller's RA0 analog input.

Microcontroller Control: The PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano reads the force sensor signal through its analog-to-digital converter (ADC). The microcontroller is intended to use this information to monitor gripping force and adjust the servo control signal.

Servo Gripper: The Kitronik Klaw Mk2 uses a servo motor to open and close the gripper. The PIC generates a PWM-based servo control signal through the SERVO_PWM connection.

Power Supply: A 9 V external input is connected to an L7805 linear voltage regulator, which provides a nominal 5 V supply for the external electronics. The PIC Curiosity Nano is powered separately through USB. The regulator's current and thermal capacity must be verified against the servo's startup and stall requirements before physical operation.

Communication and Debugging: UART_RX and UART_TX connections allow communication with other robotic arm subsystems. A debug LED, pushbutton, and test points provide additional ways to monitor and troubleshoot the circuit.

Product Requirements: This design supports the robotic arm's object-handling function by combining servo-controlled gripping, force sensing, and communication with the other subsystems. The force feedback is intended to help the system grip objects without applying excessive pressure.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This page documents the electrical power budget for Team 107's Simple Educational Robotic Arm, focusing on the Gripper and Object Handling subsystem.

The purpose of the power budget is to estimate the operating and peak current requirements of the subsystem, determine its electrical power consumption, and evaluate whether the selected power supply and voltage regulator can safely support the connected components.

The gripper subsystem includes the following major electrical components:

  • PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano microcontroller
  • Kitronik Klaw Mk2 servo-operated gripper
  • Interlink Electronics FSR 402 force sensor
  • MCP6004 operational amplifier
  • L7805 linear voltage regulator
  • Debug LED and associated resistors
  • Power connectors and supporting circuitry

The subsystem uses a nominal 9 V external power input, which passes through a fuse and an L7805 regulator to produce a nominal 5 V rail for the external circuitry. The PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano is powered separately through USB.

The calculations will account for operating current, peak current, voltage regulator power dissipation, and supply capacity. Values that have not yet been verified will be identified as estimates or pending measurements.

The final power supply suitability will be determined after verifying the servo's peak current and the regulator's thermal limitations.

docs.title: Electrical Component Power Requirements
docs.text:
Table 1: Gripper Subsystem Power Budget

Component Quantity Supply Voltage Operating Current Peak Current Power Source Kitronik Klaw Mk2 servo 1 5 V nominal TBD TBD (stall) External 5 V rail PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano 1 USB (5 V input) TBD TBD USB MCP6004 operational amplifier 1 IC 5 V nominal TBD TBD External 5 V rail FSR 402 and 10 kΩ resistor 1 circuit 5 V nominal TBD TBD External 5 V rail Debug LED and 330 Ω resistor 1 circuit 5 V nominal TBD TBD External 5 V rail L7805 voltage regulator 1 9 V input / 5 V output TBD TBD External 9 V supply

Note: The FSR 402 is a variable resistor. Its current depends on the resistance of the sensor and its voltage-divider resistor.

Current Status: The table reflects the updated schematic. Operating and peak currents must be calculated or verified before finalizing the power budget.

docs.title: Equation 1: Electrical Power
docs.text:
Electrical power is calculated using:

P = V × I

Where:

  • P = Electrical power in watts (W)
  • V = Supply voltage in volts (V)
  • I = Current in amperes (A)

For the external 5 V power supply:

P = 5 × I

For example, if a component draws 0.5 A at 5 V:

P = 5 × 0.5 = 2.5 W

This is an example calculation, not a measured component current.

docs.title: Equation 2: Total Supply Current
docs.text:
The total current drawn from the external supply is the sum of the current drawn by the servo, logic power circuitry, sensors, and other connected loads:

I_total = I_servo + I_logic_input + I_other_5V

The logic input current must include the effect of any 3.3 V regulator and its efficiency or quiescent current. Currents on different voltage rails must not simply be added without accounting for the power conversion method.

docs.title: Equation 3: Peak Current Requirement
docs.text:
The external power supply must be capable of supporting the maximum expected simultaneous current draw:

I_supply_rated >= I_total_peak

A suitable design margin should be added after verifying the actual peak currents.

docs.title: Equation 4: FSR 402 Voltage Divider Current
docs.text:
The FSR 402 is connected in a voltage-divider circuit with a 10 kΩ resistor and a nominal 5 V supply.

The current is calculated using:

I_FSR = V / (R1 + R_FSR)

Assuming the FSR resistance approaches 0 Ω under maximum force:

I_FSR,max = 5 V / (10,000 Ω + 0 Ω)

I_FSR,max = 0.0005 A = 0.5 mA

Maximum divider power:

P_FSR,max = V × I

P_FSR,max = 5 V × 0.0005 A

P_FSR,max = 0.0025 W = 2.5 mW

Therefore, the FSR voltage-divider circuit draws no more than approximately 0.5 mA from the nominal 5 V supply, assuming the stated 10 kΩ series resistance.

docs.title: Debug LED Current and Power Calculation
docs.text:
The debug LED uses a 330 Ω current-limiting resistor.

Assuming a 5 V supply and an LED forward voltage of 2 V:

I_LED = (V_supply - V_LED) / R3

I_LED = (5 V - 2 V) / 330 Ω

I_LED = 0.00909 A = 9.09 mA

The total circuit power consumption is:

P_LED = V_supply × I_LED

P_LED = 5 V × 0.00909 A

P_LED = 0.0455 W = 45.5 mW

The estimated debug LED circuit current is 9.09 mA when the LED is on, assuming a 5 V drive voltage.

This is a preliminary estimate. The actual current and power source depend on the PIC output voltage and the LED forward voltage.

docs.title: MCP6004 Operational Amplifier Power Calculation
docs.text:
The MCP6004 is a quad operational amplifier used to condition the FSR 402 force sensor signal.

For this preliminary calculation, the typical supply current is estimated as 100 µA per amplifier.

Total estimated current:

I_MCP6004 = 4 × 100 µA

I_MCP6004 = 400 µA = 0.4 mA

Power consumption at 5 V:

P_MCP6004 = V × I

P_MCP6004 = 5 V × 0.0004 A

P_MCP6004 = 0.002 W = 2 mW

The MCP6004 is estimated to consume approximately 0.4 mA and 2 mW under typical conditions.

These values are preliminary estimates and must be checked against the component datasheet. The final power budget must also consider worst-case supply current and output loading.

docs.title: Kitronik Klaw Mk2 Servo Power Calculation
docs.text:
Manufacturer: Kitronik Part Number: 25104 Included Motor: Mini 180-degree servo Specified Operating Voltage: 3 V to 6 V Design Supply Voltage: 5 V

The servo operates the robotic gripper by opening and closing its jaws.

Electrical power is calculated using:

P = V × I

Operating power: P_operating = 5 V × I_operating

Peak stall power: P_stall = 5 V × I_stall

The manufacturer confirms the operating voltage range but does not specify operating or stall current in the published kit specifications.

Operating Current: TBD Stall Current: TBD Operating Power: TBD Peak Power: TBD

The current requirements must be verified before confirming the suitability of the L7805 regulator.

Source: https://kitronik.co.uk/products/25104-klaw-mk2-robotic-gripper-kit

docs.title: L7805 Voltage Regulator Power Dissipation
docs.text:
The gripper subsystem uses an L7805 linear voltage regulator to convert the external 9 V supply to a nominal 5 V output.

Input Voltage = 9 V Output Voltage = 5 V

Voltage drop:

V_drop = 9 V - 5 V = 4 V

Approximate regulator power dissipation:

P_regulator = (V_in - V_out) × I_load

P_regulator = 4 V × I_load

Example calculations:

Load Current Regulator Power Dissipation 100 mA 0.4 W 250 mA 1.0 W 500 mA 2.0 W 750 mA 3.0 W 1000 mA 4.0 W

The L7805 dissipates the voltage difference between its input and output as heat.

The regulator's thermal suitability depends on the total load current, ambient temperature, package, and available heatsinking.

The servo's operating and stall current must be verified before the regulator can be approved for the final design.

These values are examples, not measured load currents.

docs.title: Total Subsystem Current and Power
docs.text:
The total current requirement is calculated by combining the loads connected to the external regulated 5 V supply.

Preliminary known loads:

MCP6004 amplifier = 0.40 mA FSR 402 voltage divider = 0.50 mA maximum

Combined estimated current:

I_known = 0.40 + 0.50

I_known = 0.90 mA

Combined estimated power:

P_known = 5 V × 0.0009 A

P_known = 0.0045 W = 4.5 mW

The servo current has not yet been verified.

Total external current:

I_external = I_servo + I_other_external_loads

The debug LED supply connection must be verified before including it in the external load total.

The PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano is powered separately through USB and is not included in the external 9 V supply current.

The external supply current and regulator power dissipation cannot be finalized until the servo's operating and peak current requirements are known.

The 0.90 mA value is a preliminary subtotal, not the complete subsystem current requirement.

docs.title: Calculation Status
docs.text: The final total current and power requirements are pending confirmation of the MG90S servo current, PIC board power consumption, sensor module current, regulator configuration, and external power supply current rating.

docs.title: External Power Supply Selection
docs.text:
The Gripper & Object Handling subsystem is designed to use an external 9 V DC power supply.

The external 9 V input passes through a 1 A fuse before reaching the L7805 linear voltage regulator.

The L7805 provides a nominal 5 V output for the external gripper and sensor circuitry.

The PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano is powered separately through its USB connection.

docs.title: Power Supply Requirements

docs.title: Supply Power Calculation
docs.text:
The available input power is calculated using:

P_supply = V_supply × I_supply

P_supply = 9 V × I_supply

For illustration, a 9 V supply rated at 1 A would provide up to 9 W of rated input power.

This is an example, not confirmation that the selected power supply has a 1 A rating.

docs.title: Voltage Regulator Considerations
docs.text:
The L7805 drops approximately 4 V between its input and output.

P_regulator ≈ 4 V × I_load

The regulator dissipates this power as heat.

The regulator's output current capability depends on its thermal conditions and component ratings.

The 1 A input fuse does not guarantee that the regulator or servo is protected against all overcurrent or overheating conditions.

docs.title: Current Status
docs.text:
The 9 V input and 5 V regulated output match the intended schematic architecture.

However, the external supply current rating, servo peak current, and regulator thermal performance still require verification.

The final power supply suitability cannot yet be confirmed.

docs.title: Candidate Supply Calculation
docs.text:
P = V x I

P = 5 V x 3 A = 15 W

A 5 V, 3 A supply can provide up to 15 W of rated output power. This does not mean the robotic arm continuously consumes 15 W.

Supply Status: Candidate only; not yet selected or verified.

Before final selection, the combined peak current of all connected subsystems must be calculated, including the MG90S servo and microcontroller circuitry. Appropriate current margin, wiring capacity, and protection must also be considered.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
The updated power budget documents the electrical requirements of Team 107's Gripper & Object Handling subsystem.

The design uses an external 9 V DC supply and an L7805 linear voltage regulator to provide a nominal 5 V rail for the gripper and associated electronics.

The PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano is powered separately through USB.

The preliminary calculations indicate:

  • FSR voltage-divider maximum current: 0.50 mA
  • MCP6004 estimated typical current: 0.40 mA
  • Combined preliminary current: 0.90 mA
  • Combined preliminary power: 4.5 mW
  • Regulator voltage drop: 4 V
  • Regulator dissipation: approximately 4 W per ampere of 5 V load current

The debug LED current has been estimated separately, pending confirmation of its actual drive voltage.

The Kitronik Klaw Mk2 servo is expected to be a major electrical load. Its operating and stall current requirements remain unverified.

Before the design is finalized, the servo current, external power supply rating, regulator thermal performance, and actual wiring connections must be confirmed.

Final Status: Preliminary power budget calculations completed. Final supply and regulator suitability remain pending verification.

Final Status: Preliminary power budget completed; numerical current verification and final supply selection remain pending.
